column3: Repeats the full closing formula after David's forgiveness, directly joining restored nearness with an excellent return.
Gives the same excellent return to believers who do good, extending the focus from David to a durable moral pattern.
Names an excellent return for the reverent within the same surah's exemplary-servant sequence.
The return-place for transgressors supplies the adverse outcome against which the focus's excellent return is defined.
God's treasuries and measured bestowal help distinguish divine source and custody from the worth of worldly means.
Locating even hostile schemes with God adds divine oversight as a context for the focus's evaluative "with Us."
Its evil return for transgressors is the immediate same-surah contrast to the excellent return in the focus.
Grace from God illustrates beneficent divine relation, but does not specify nearness or an excellent return.
Mercy from God after affliction parallels restoration, yet lacks the focus's explicit nearness and final return.
The universal return to God clarifies the ultimate direction that the focus calls excellent for David.
The wish for an earlier reminder does not illuminate David's nearness or return.
Paradise being brought near pictures an eschatological nearness, though it is not the focus's personal divine nearness.
It denies that wealth and children bring nearness, except through faith and good works, directly revaluing status in the focus's terms.
The drawing-near of Paradise supplies an eschatological counterpart to the focus's honored nearness.
It repeats the Paradise-nearness image already supplied by 50:31 with less added detail.
It contrasts false claimed access to God with unavoidable accounting before the true Lord.
A good reward in the hereafter supports the positive outcome, but not the focus's nearness or return formula.
Solomon's gift and his being an oft-returning servant place the focus within the Davidic succession rather than worldly inheritance alone.
Good companionship after obedience is a broad positive end without clarifying divine nearness.
The promise to every preserving returner makes repeated turning the character that receives the promised end.
Bringing others near in the sea narrative has no useful relation to divine nearness or return.
God alone holding knowledge offers only a general sense of divine possession, not the focus's honor.
The irresistibility of punishment does not clarify David's nearness or return.
The two possible outcomes of conflict do not clarify the focus's final evaluation.
God's ownership of creation adds no specific contribution to nearness or an excellent return.
Its use of "at" for ritual practice by the House is unrelated to the focus.
Divine power over harm and good does not specify the honored return at issue.
Exclusive worship, calling to God, and returning to Him form a direct orientation toward the return named excellent in the focus.
The chosen excellence of earlier prophets "with Us" closely parallels David's honored standing.
The Garden of Refuge near the lote tree offers a distant spatial image, not the focus's evaluative nearness.
Victory for God's forces does not clarify David's personal nearness or return.
A divine measure of time is unrelated to the focus's excellent return.
The Quran's exalted status with God only broadly echoes the locative formulation.
The condemnation of prohibited acts does not add to the focus's positive outcome.
The comparison of provisions has no material connection to the focus.
The birds' shared turning within David's narrative illuminates the return-oriented language surrounding his honor.
An unending reward is a broad positive counterpart but lacks nearness and return.
Knowledge of the Hour does not clarify David's standing with God.
Gardens of bliss with their Lord give the reverent a lasting blessed state near the divine source.
Job's praise as a patient, oft-returning servant supplies another same-surah model of the trait underlying the focus's good end.
Humble, eager worship offers a general devotional disposition without the focus's final honor.
Both worldly and afterlife reward being with God modestly supports the relocation of value from immediate aims.
Mercy and knowledge given to a servant do not clarify the focus's nearness or return.
David's strength and repeated return, introduced immediately before his account, explain the character whose final honor is announced.
Calling truth from God magic concerns rejection, not David's honored return.
God's severe judgment of words without deeds clarifies that divine evaluation, not public standing, governs worth.
What people possess perishes while what is with God endures, sharply recasting lasting value in the focus's direction.
The dispute about patriarchal identities does not illuminate the focus.
Rejection of revelation as magic does not clarify divine nearness or return.
It makes taking a return-route to one's Lord a chosen orientation, complementing the focus's excellent destination.
A mistaken wish about death has no useful relation to the focus.
Forgiveness for those who repeatedly return explicitly connects restored moral orientation with the focus's positive end.
Submission and goodness receive reward with the Lord, generalizing the ethical basis for a blessed outcome.
The rhetorical denial of access to the unseen does not clarify honored nearness.
It contrasts worldly attractions with the excellent return that is with God, directly framing the focus's revaluation of worldly goods.
Joseph's restriction on access to his court has no useful relation to the focus.
God's preservation of costly good deeds and the finest reward adds an enduring reward logic to the excellent return.
Mention before an earthly master does not illuminate divine nearness.
The doers of good receive what they desire with their Lord, supplying a concrete blessed outcome.
False intercessors claimed as a means of nearness to God contrast with the authentic nearness granted in the focus.
It exposes worship of intermediaries for supposed nearness to God, a direct boundary for the focus's granted nearness.
Dispute before the Lord establishes accountability but adds little after the clearer return and reward cards.
Belief and humility before revealed truth do not specify the focus's final honor.
The dwelling of peace with their Lord presents a settled, protected end for the rightly guided.
Inheritance rules do not clarify divine nearness or an excellent return.
The location of judgment and punishment does not contribute to the focus's honor.
Attributing events to God in Pharaoh's story does not clarify David's return.
The challenge about possessing the unseen is unrelated to the focus.
Return to God and the fire for the excessive provide a negative moral outcome against the focus's excellent return.
Control of signs and refusal to believe do not clarify the focus's divine nearness.
God's exclusive power to remove harm and bestow favor is too general to add to the focus.
The denial of human control over God's treasuries only loosely bears on revaluing worldly power.
Provision from God illustrates divine giving without the focus's nearness or return.
Constant service by those with the Lord presents an active form of honored divine proximity.
Good deeds erasing evil offer a limited moral parallel to restoration after fault.
A covenant with the Merciful limits intercession, but does not explain the focus's granted nearness.
The incomplete statement adds no discernible relation to the focus.
The refusal of an unjust substitution in Joseph's story is unrelated to the focus.
Its correction of causal attribution does not clarify the focus's final honor.
A claimed covenant with the Merciful is a distant contrast to God-granted standing.
What good one sends ahead is found with God, better and greater in reward, supporting lasting divine valuation.
The brothers' account of leaving Joseph at their goods is unrelated to the focus.
The sinner's presumptive claim to the best with his Lord contrasts with the focus's declared, not assumed, honor.
Temporal nearness of the promised event is not the divine nearness in the focus.
Universal glorification and forgiveness give only a broad devotional background.
Reverence near the Messenger yields forgiveness and reward, but does not clarify the focus's divine nearness.
The long account of corruption and judgment does not add to David's final standing.
It contrasts possessions and children as a trial with the great reward held by God, reinforcing the focus's revaluation of resources.
Inheritance legislation does not illuminate the focus.
Gardens, enduring pleasure, and mutual satisfaction with the Lord give a full image of the blessed end.
The statement of divine might and mercy does not specifically clarify the focus.
What is with God is better than diversion and trade, directly subordinating transient economic gain to lasting divine value.
A better resting place for the Garden's companions is a broad parallel to an excellent return.
A secure seat with an all-powerful sovereign gives a vivid image of protected honored proximity.
The brothers' appeal to Joseph's goodness is unrelated to the focus.
God's treasuries versus material pressure near the Messenger only indirectly bears on the focus's valuation of means.
Sincere devotion in danger followed by association contrasts genuine reorientation with its abandonment.
The timing of punishment in the messenger's possession does not clarify the focus.
Its spatial location at the lote tree has no useful relation to David's honored nearness.
The denial of reciprocal human favor does not explain divine nearness or an excellent return.
David recognizes the test, seeks forgiveness, falls in submission, and turns back, directly supplying the repentance behind his restored honor.
David's earthly vicegerency is bound to truthful judgment and resistance to desire, defining how authority is reoriented before the focus's final evaluation.
Solomon asks forgiveness before receiving unmatched dominion, directly contrasting bestowed rule with the return-oriented standing shared in this narrative.
God calls Solomon's wealth and power a gift to dispense, making authority an entrusted means rather than the enduring value named in the focus.
The chosen servants are distinguished by remembrance of the final abode, explicitly joining exemplary status to orientation toward return.
Open gardens of lasting residence unfold the excellent return named for the reverent in the same passage.
The promised provision for the Day of Account confirms that the righteous end is a settled divine commitment.
The foremost are identified as those brought near, giving a direct wider Quranic category for honored divine proximity.
The close servant's rest, provision, and Garden of bliss provide a concrete outcome for privileged nearness.
Faithful expenditure is counted as means of nearness to God, showing a practical orientation toward the proximity granted in the focus.
The angels brought near are honored through unremitting servitude, supporting nearness as a relational rank rather than worldly authority.
God's response to the caller supplies a broad form of divine closeness, though not the focus's post-forgiveness honor.
